opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that we're still quite early, even though it feels like a lot has happened. From my side, having worked mostly on the infrastructure side of RL, the first thing I'd say is that progress is going to be bottlenecked less by clever new algorithms and more by engineering: how fast you can iterate, how reliably your system runs at scale, and how quickly you can find and fix bugs. In RL especially, a tiny bug in how rewards are computed or how data flows between the sampler and the trainer can silently ruin a run, and you might not notice for days. So I think a lot of the real progress comes from people who build very solid, very fast infrastructure and then just run many, many experiments.

The second thing is the environment and the reward. For large models, the policy is already very strong from pretraining, so the question becomes: what tasks do you give it, and how do you tell it whether it did well? Verifiable domains like math and code worked first because the reward is clean. The harder and more interesting direction is extending that to messier tasks, like long-horizon agentic work, research-like tasks, or things where "good" is partly subjective. Building good environments and good graders is, I think, underrated work, and it's where a lot of the leverage is going to be.

Third, I'd encourage people not to over-index on whatever method is popular right now. Every few months there's a new acronym, but many of these variants end up performing about the same once you control for the details. What really matters is understanding your system end to end, measuring carefully, and being willing to simplify. Often the simple baseline, scaled up properly, beats the fancy idea.

And finally, at a more personal level, I think the people who will push this forward are those who are curious and willing to get their hands dirty. You can read papers all day, but in RL you really learn by running things, watching them fail, and figuring out why. So my advice would be: build things, keep the feedback loop short, and stay honest about what's actually working.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest starting point is that the "exploration" we talk about in classic RL and the exploration problem for large models are only loosely the same thing. In the classic setting, the agent starts from nothing, and the whole challenge is getting any signal at all in a sparse environment. With a pretrained language model, you already have a prior that's quite strong. The model has seen a huge amount of human reasoning and code and so on, so when it samples, it's not sampling randomly, it's sampling plausible attempts. That changes the question from "how do we discover anything" to "how do we stop the model from collapsing onto the handful of strategies it already prefers."

So if you ask me where it should go, a few things.

First, I think we're underusing the structure of the problem. Right now most RL for LLMs is essentially: sample a bunch of completions, score them with a verifier or a reward model, push the probability mass toward the good ones. That works surprisingly well, but the exploration is almost entirely coming from temperature and from the pretraining prior. There's very little deliberate exploration. The things that actually drove progress in Atari and Go, like curiosity signals, count-based or density-based novelty, structured search, those have barely been translated. Part of that is scale. Running MCTS on a reasoning trace is expensive. But I think the bigger reason is that it's just hard to define "novelty" in the space of natural language. Two completions can be worded totally differently and be the same idea. If we can get a decent notion of semantic diversity, I think a lot of the old ideas become usable again.

Second, I'd push on the environment side rather than the algorithm side. I spent a lot of time on infrastructure, and my feeling is that the bottleneck for exploration is less about which policy gradient estimator you use and more about whether the model has somewhere interesting to explore. Verifiable domains like math and code are great because the reward is clean, but they're also narrow. You get models that are very good at competition problems and then you ask what the equivalent of that is for, say, a long research task or a multi-step agentic workflow where the feedback is delayed and noisy. We need environments that are rich enough that there's a real frontier to push on, and that means a lot of unglamorous engineering: simulators, sandboxes, tool-use setups, ways to generate tasks at scale with reliable grading.

Third, I think we need to be more honest about what counts as exploration versus what counts as reward hacking. When a model finds a clever shortcut that the verifier didn't anticipate, in some sense that's exactly what exploration is supposed to produce. The problem is we can't tell the difference between a genuinely new solution and a loophole until we look. So the research on exploration has to go hand in hand with better evaluation and with reward models that are robust to distribution shift. Otherwise you just get very creative cheating.

And then the last point, which is a bit more speculative: I suspect the most interesting exploration won't happen within a single rollout but across training. Things like letting the model generate its own curricula, or doing some kind of population-based training where different models are pushed toward different regions, or just being more careful about the KL constraint and entropy so we don't prematurely sharpen the distribution. Right now a lot of training runs quietly lose entropy and nobody treats that as the central failure mode, but I think it is. If the model stops being able to surprise itself, it stops learning.

So in short: better notions of diversity in language space, much richer environments, evaluation that can actually distinguish discovery from exploitation, and treating the collapse of the policy as the thing to fight rather than an afterthought. Less about a fancier algorithm, more about building the conditions where exploration has a chance to pay off.

astra-6.text:
I think we should explore it along two tracks. One is to work in settings where we can evaluate the outcome clearly, so we can understand what reinforcement learning actually improves. The other is to tackle more open-ended tasks, where defining a good reward is itself part of the research problem.

In both cases, I’d want to distinguish getting better at the training task from learning something that transfers. If we change the environment, or give the model a problem that requires a longer sequence of decisions, does the improvement hold up? And how much does that improvement depend on the starting model, the feedback, and the amount of exploration?

So I’d encourage ambitious experiments alongside smaller, controlled studies. We need to push performance, but we also need to understand which choices are responsible for the gains. That understanding will help us decide where to go next.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should explore it along two tracks. One is to work on problems where we can verify the outcome, like coding or math. That gives us a clearer signal and lets us study what reinforcement learning actually improves. Is the model learning a new strategy? Is it using tools better? Or is it just getting better at producing answers that receive a high reward?

The other track is to move toward more open-ended tasks, where success is harder to define. There, the reward itself becomes a central research problem. We need to understand how to capture what people want without encouraging the model to exploit weaknesses in the feedback.

Across both tracks, I’d like to see more careful experiments on exploration: whether models discover different approaches, how much diversity we lose during training, and whether improvements transfer to unfamiliar problems. Higher benchmark scores are useful, but the bigger question is whether we’re building models that can adapt when the task changes.
